auditor_value: net force = m a = 65 N along the belt's acceleration (supplied by static friction); a_max = mu_s g = 0.2 x 9.8 = 1.96 m/s^2

findings.quote: Multiplying the mass by the maximum acceleration formula's coefficient alone (μₛ × mass) instead of μₛ × g gives 13 N as a wrong 'maximum force', confusing the force limit with the acceleration limit.
findings.note: Vague and hard to read: it describes multiplying a coefficient by a mass and calling the product a force, which is not a recognisable student error on this question, and the sentence uses quotation marks and a formula-of-a-formula phrasing. The arithmetic (0.2 x 65 = 13) does follow, but the entry does not name a genuine mistake clearly.
findings.fix: Forgetting that the maximum friction force is μₛ m g = 0.2 × 65 × 9.8 = 127.4 N, and instead reporting the net force 65 N as the maximum friction the belt can supply.

findings.note: Not a physics concept; the solution uses no pseudo force or non-inertial frame (it works in the ground frame).
findings.fix: remove the tag, or replace with 'limiting friction'

notes: Answer agrees. In the ground frame the man's only horizontal force is static friction, so f = m a = 65 N; slipping starts when m a exceeds mu_s m g. g = 9.8 as the question fixes; the first common-mistake entry (2.0 m/s^2 with g = 10) is genuine.
